Nemesis

/NEM-uh-sis/ — stress on the first syllable · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A nemesis is a longtime rival or enemy who seems especially difficult to defeat or overcome.

For years, that debate team was our team's nemesis.

Worked Example

Every season, when the elite volleyball team from across town arrived at the regional tournament, our school's team felt the weight of facing them — year after year, that team seemed to find a way to beat us, no matter our preparation.

This team is more than just an enemy or a rival; nemesis captures both the history of battles between the teams and the sense that they're especially hard to defeat. Just saying 'rival' would miss that special quality of being your 'signature struggle.'

How Nemesis Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

rival

rival: someone competing with you for the same prize

opponent

opponent: the person you face in a contest

scourge

scourge: a cause of great suffering or trouble

Antonyms

friend

friend: someone who likes and supports you warmly

ally

ally: a partner who fights on your side

How Strong Is It? — rival → opponent → foe → nemesis

rival vs. nemesis

rival vs. nemesis: A rival is simply someone chasing the same goal as you, so it is much weaker than Nemesis, which names an enemy who defeats you over and over.

opponent vs. nemesis

opponent vs. nemesis: An opponent is whoever happens to stand against you in one contest, which makes it clearly weaker than Nemesis, an enemy you can never seem to shake.

foe vs. nemesis

foe vs. nemesis: Calling someone a foe signals real hostility, yet even foe is weaker than Nemesis, the one foe who beats you again and again no matter how you prepare.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — nemesis

Root — nemesis: a long-standing opponent or source of deserved ruin; originally, the Greek goddess of retribution (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Nemesis came into English as one whole piece: it is the name of the Greek goddess of retribution, who tracked people down and delivered exactly the ruin they had earned — and no one could escape her. That is why a nemesis today is not just any competitor, but the long-standing opponent who keeps handing you the defeat you cannot avoid. And the word can still grow: attach the prefix arch-, meaning 'chief' or 'most extreme,' and you get arch-nemesis — the one great rival who stands above all the rest.

Use the root in a new word: arch-nemesis

Use the root in a new word: arch-nemesis: The prefix arch- means 'chief' or 'most extreme' — the same arch- you hear in archenemy and archrival. Combine it with nemesis, a longtime opponent who is especially hard to defeat, and arch-nemesis names someone's ultimate, most formidable opponent: the one rival above all others.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Nemesis is a grand, mythic word — your nemesis isn't just any rival, but the one you've struggled against repeatedly and who seems almost destined to defeat you. For everyday competition, 'rival' or 'opponent' is simpler. But when you want to capture that sense of an almost-fated struggle, nemesis is the word that lands.
